title: Distributed Cache
seoTitle: Design a Distributed Cache Like Redis or Memcached
description: Design a distributed in-memory cache — get/set/delete with TTL, LRU eviction, consistent hashing, replication and hot-key handling.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Understanding the Problem

blocks.title: What is a Distributed Cache?
blocks.text: A distributed cache is an in-memory key-value store spread across many machines. Applications put frequently read data in it to avoid slower databases — think Redis Cluster or Memcached.
Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Clients should be able to `set`, `get`, and `delete` key-value pairs.
Clients should be able to set an expiration (TTL) on a key.
When memory is full, the cache should evict entries using an LRU policy.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

items: Rich data structures (lists, sets, sorted sets).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

blocks.text: Non-Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Operations should be extremely fast: < 10ms at p99, typically sub-millisecond on the server.
The cache should hold ~1TB of data and serve ~100M requests per second.
The system should be highly available and tolerate node failures; eventual consistency between replicas is acceptable.
It should scale horizontally by adding nodes.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):
The Set Up
Planning the Approach
We'll first design a single cache node that does get, set, TTL and LRU correctly, then work out how to spread data across many nodes and survive failures.
Defining the Core Entities

items: **Entry metadata**: expiration timestamp and recency information for LRU.

blocks.text: API or System Interface
Real caches use a compact binary or text protocol over long-lived TCP connections (like RESP for Redis) rather than HTTP — per-request HTTP overhead would dominate sub-millisecond operations.
High-Level Design
1) Clients should be able to get, set and delete
A single node keeps everything in a **hash map** from key to entry, giving O(1) average lookups. A server process accepts connections and executes commands against the map.
2) Keys should expire after their TTL
Store an `expiresAt` timestamp with each entry. Use two complementary mechanisms:

items: **Lazy expiration**: on `get`, if the entry is expired, delete it and return a miss.
**Active expiration**: a background task periodically samples keys with TTLs and deletes expired ones, so memory isn't held by keys nobody reads.

blocks.text: 3) The cache should evict least-recently-used entries

Pair the hash map with a **doubly linked list** ordered by recency. Every `get` or `set` moves the entry's node to the head; when memory exceeds the limit, evict from the tail. Both operations are O(1) because the map holds a pointer to each list node.

blocks.caption: Single node: hash map + LRU list

blocks.text: Potential Deep Dives
1) How do we spread data across many nodes?
1TB doesn't fit on one machine, and 100M requests per second needs many CPUs. We need to partition keys across nodes.

approach.text: Route each key to node `hash(key) % N`.

challenges.text: Adding or removing a single node changes N, which remaps almost every key. The cache is effectively flushed, and the database behind it gets a stampede of misses.

approach.text: Place nodes on a hash ring; each key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash. Adding or removing a node only moves the keys in its arc (~1/N of the data). Giving each physical node many **virtual nodes** on the ring evens out load and lets bigger machines take more tokens.

challenges.text: Clients (or a proxy) must know the current ring. Membership changes are propagated via a coordination service (e.g. ZooKeeper/etcd) or gossip, and clients refresh their view.

blocks.text: 2) How do we survive node failures?

approach.text: If a node dies, its keys are simply gone; consistent hashing sends those keys to the next node, which misses and refills from the database.

challenges.text: A large node failing causes a burst of misses and database load. Acceptable for small clusters, risky at our scale.

blocks.title: Primary-replica per shard with automatic failover

approach.text: Each shard has a primary and one or more replicas. Writes go to the primary and replicate **asynchronously** (we chose availability over consistency). Health checks detect a failed primary and promote a replica; clients update their routing.

challenges.text: Async replication can lose the last few writes on failover — fine for a cache. Split-brain must be prevented with a quorum-based failure detector.

blocks.text: 3) How do we handle hot keys?
A single viral key can send millions of requests per second to one shard.

approach.text: Detect hot keys (sampling request counts) and store copies under suffixed keys like `key#1..key#k` on different shards; readers pick one at random. Writes update all copies.

challenges.text: Writes become k times more expensive and copies can briefly diverge.

blocks.title: Client-side near cache for hot keys

approach.text: Clients keep a tiny local in-process cache with a short TTL (e.g. 1-5 seconds) for keys flagged as hot. Most reads never leave the application server.

challenges.text: Values can be stale for up to the local TTL. Combine with server-side hot-key replication for the most extreme cases.

blocks.text: Final Design

quiz.question: Which pair of data structures gives O(1) get and O(1) LRU eviction?
quiz.explanation: The map finds the entry instantly; the linked list lets you move it to the head or evict the tail in constant time.

quiz.question: Why does modulo hashing work poorly when nodes are added or removed?
options: Changing N remaps almost every key
quiz.explanation: hash % N depends on N, so a membership change moves most keys and effectively flushes the cache.

quiz.question: What do virtual nodes add to consistent hashing?
options: More even load distribution across physical nodes
quiz.explanation: Many tokens per machine smooth out the arcs each node owns.

quiz.question: Why is lazy expiration alone not enough for TTLs?
options: Expired keys that are never read would keep using memory
quiz.explanation: A background sweeper reclaims memory from expired keys nobody reads.
